power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "p<2.75", Text = "Collapsed variant carrier status was strongly associated with hallmark HA20 phenotypes, including Behçet's disease (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 23466.7; 95% CI, 987-557936), gastrointestinal ulcers with hemorrhage (aOR, 227.1; 95% CI, 13.6-3796.6), and oral aphthae (aOR, 188.8; 95% CI, 19.3-1841.2), surpassing a Bonferroni-corrected significance threshold (p<2.75×10 )."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. text.text: Monogenic diseases are considered rare, yet many remain underdiagnosed when clinical manifestations are heterogeneous.
A20 haploinsufficiency (HA20) is an early-onset inborn error of immunity (IEI) caused by heterozygous TNFAIP3 variants that dysregulate inflammatory signaling, producing diverse immune phenotypes.
We analyzed variants in all human haploinsufficiency (HI) disease genes in gnomAD, All of Us (AoU), and UK Biobank (UKBB), applying refined loss-of-function predictors.
Rare TNFAIP3 variants (allele frequency <0.01%) were classified as predicted loss-of-function (pLOF) or functionally validated highly predicted pathogenic missense (fHPPM).
text.formatted: Rare TNFAIP3 variants (allele frequency <0.01%) were classified as predicted loss-of-function (pLOF) or functionally validated highly predicted pathogenic missense (fHPPM).

text.text: Clinical associations were tested through meta-phenome-wide association studies (PheWAS) and phenome-set enrichment analysis (PSEA) and, for TNFAIP3, validated in a University of Pittsburgh referral cohort and a single center biobank at Mass General Brigham (MGB).
Deleterious variants in human HI disease genes, including IEI-HI genes, occurred frequently despite strong constraint and were significantly associated with immune disease risk.
TNFAIP3 pLOF variant prevalences were as high as ~1:24,000; combined pLOF + fHPPM prevalences reached ~1:9,000.
PheWAS and PSEA linked rare TNFAIP3 variants to diverse immune phenotypes.
In a referral cohort (18 patients, 9 families), missense variants conferred hypomorphism with intermediate immunophenotypes.

In the MGB biobank, 29 individuals carried hypomorphic TNFAIP3 variants without a HA20 diagnosis; nearly two-thirds had phenotypes consistent with or plausibly related to A20 hypomorphism, suggesting penetrance exceeds 50%.
Only 4 had received HA20-directed immunomodulatory therapy.
Deleterious IEI-HI variants are far more common than reported and are associated with immune dysregulation; hypomorphic TNFAIP3 variants are common and highly penetrant with variable expressivity.
Genotype-first analysis of institutional biobanks can identify untreated IEI-HI patients.
These findings establish proof-of-concept that haploinsufficiency diseases are pervasively underrecognized.
Patients with early-onset or treatment-refractory immune disease should be prioritized for genetic testing; biobank callback amendments may expedite diagnosis, monitoring, and precision therapy.
Monogenic conditions are often assumed to be rare.
Recent work suggests that many could be underdiagnosed and their collective population prevalence underestimated, particularly for disorders with heterogeneous clinical phenotypes 1 .
text.formatted: Recent work suggests that many could be underdiagnosed and their collective population prevalence underestimated, particularly for disorders with heterogeneous clinical phenotypes <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1</ref> .

text.text: However, prior studies have focused on incompletely penetrant alleles with well-defined phenotypes and have lacked definitive validation in independent clinical cohorts 2, 3 .
text.formatted: However, prior studies have focused on incompletely penetrant alleles with well-defined phenotypes and have lacked definitive validation in independent clinical cohorts <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3</ref> .

text.text: The relevance of these findings to heterogeneous immune conditions and the links between population-wide variant burden and clinical disease burden remain unclear.
One such monogenic disease, A20 haploinsufficiency (HA20), is an early onset inflammatory syndrome caused by high penetrance, heterozygous germline variants in TNFAIP3 4 .
text.formatted: One such monogenic disease, A20 haploinsufficiency (HA20), is an early onset inflammatory syndrome caused by high penetrance, heterozygous germline variants in TNFAIP3 <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4</ref> .

text.text: TNFAIP3 encodes the multifunctional ubiquitin-editing enzyme A20 5, 6 .
text.formatted: TNFAIP3 encodes the multifunctional ubiquitin-editing enzyme A20 <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6</ref> .

text.text: HA20 patients exhibit dysregulation of TNF-NF-κB, inflammasome, and interferon signaling pathways and present with diverse phenotypes including autoinflammation, autoimmunity, lymphoproliferation, and recurrent infection 7.
text.formatted: HA20 patients exhibit dysregulation of TNF-NF-κB, inflammasome, and interferon signaling pathways and present with diverse phenotypes including autoinflammation, autoimmunity, lymphoproliferation, and recurrent infection <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7</ref>.

text.text: Since its discovery, HA20 has been considered ultra-rare with fewer than 200 reported cases 7, 8 , most involving frameshift, truncating, deletion, or splice variants.

text.text: Missense variants are reported to cause HA20 but are challenging to validate in the absence of clinically standardized assays, leading to potential under-ascertainment.
Moreover, genetic sequencing is not universally accessible, and older patients are often diagnosed only through family based segregation testing 8 .

text.text: Together, these factors introduce substantial ascertainment bias and lead to missed opportunities for intervention.

We hypothesized that HA20 prevalence is substantially underestimated in the U.S. and globally, and that rigorous validation through functional, clinical, and population-scale analyses could have broad implications for haploinsufficient immune diseases.
We quantified the prevalence and clinical impact of deleterious variants predicted to cause haploinsufficiency disease at U.S. and global population levels.
Focusing on TNFAIP3 variants across three population resources, we applied rare variant collapsing phenome-wide association studies (PheWAS) to uncover strong associations with immune disease.

We validated these findings through functional characterization of variants, deep immunophenotyping of a University of Pittsburgh referral cohort, and analysis of the Mass General Brigham (MGB) hospital-based biobank, providing rigorous, multimodal evidence that a heterogeneous immune disease is underrecognized and establishing proof-of-concept for underrecognition of haploinsufficiency diseases at the population level.

While population-scale biobank analysis revealed significant associations, and the Pittsburgh cohort validated missense variant effects, neither directly addressed whether genotype-first identification of HA20 and related IEI-HI disorders is clinically actionable.
We therefore interrogated the Mass General Brigham (MGB) Biobank, in which 67,576 individuals were prospectively enrolled and underwent next-generation sequencing linked to detailed EHR.

As in population biobanks, individuals with pathogenic TNFAIP3 variants were unexpectedly common: 3 with pLOF variants, 21 with hypomorphic Pittsburgh cohort variants (18 with c.1033T>C, p.Tyr345His), and 14 with HPPM variants (5 fHPPM).

text.text: Monogenic diseases are generally assumed to be rare in human populations: even the most common and incompletely penetrant haploinsufficient IEI have been reported in only ~400-500 individuals globally 39 .

text.text: However, these assumptions rely on case series rather than systematic epidemiological studies, making it impossible to reliably estimate disease prevalence.

While some recent studies have suggested higher-than-expected prevalence of pathogenic variants in population databases, definitive evidence linking variant burden to clinical disease burden has been lacking.
We found that IEI-HI genes harbored more predicted deleterious variants in population databases than expected from constraint metrics or published case counts.

Most of these genes were strongly and significantly associated with individual immune phenotypes and with collective disease burden at a population level, suggesting that these deleterious variants are not only collectively more common than expected but that they are driving a substantial burden of as-yet unrecognized genetic disease.

To more rigorously test whether this discrepancy reflects true underdiagnosis of clinical disease, we focused on TNFAIP3, where loss-of-function variants cause HA20 with reportedly complete penetrance.
Despite fewer than 200 cases worldwide, we identified deleterious TNFAIP3 variants at prevalences as high as 1:24,000, over 100-fold higher than expected.
Using unbiased phenome-wide analyses of EHR data, we found that hypomorphic variants significantly increased the odds of immune-mediated and inflammatory conditions.
These associations were further supported by deep phenotyping of HA20 patients with missense variants in our referralbased cohort.
Functional validation confirmed that identified variants impair A20 function through loss of protein activity, reduced expression, or both.
These findings suggest a substantial recognition gap for HA20 and likely for other IEI-HI diseases.
Rare missense variants have previously been reported to cause HA20, but the molecular mechanisms are poorly defined [40] [41] [42] .

text.text: Our results help resolve these contradictions by showing that missense TNFAIP3 mutations are associated with an "intermediate" immunologic phenotype, with inflammatory biomarkers attenuated relative to pLOF variants but elevated compared to healthy individuals.

Functional testing suggests that pLOF alleles uniformly impair A20 function and basal expression, while missense variants exhibit heterogeneous mechanisms; some behave like pLOF alleles, others exhibit weakly hypomorphic function, and still others reduce A20 expression despite near-normal NF-κB suppression.
Consistent with these molecular findings, deleterious missense variants are associated with a more diffuse and less specific spectrum of immune disease than LOF variants.
Although effect sizes are lower for missense variants than for LOF variants, they far exceed the effect sizes of common risk alleles.
Moreover, in a hospital-based population, >50% of carriers for the relatively common missense variant c.1033T>C (p.Tyr345His; MAF 0.012-0.02%) have phenotypes plausibly attributed to HA20.

text.text: The further observation that individuals with deleterious missense variants can develop clinically significant dominantly inherited familial immune dysregulation suggests that such patients should be monitored closely, with a low threshold to consider therapies targeting A20-regulated pathways.
A central challenge in rare variant research has been insufficient power to detect disease associations in population databases.
Prior studies have addressed this by analyzing variants with higher allele frequencies (up to 2%) or by restricting analyses to prespecified phenotypes 3 .

text.text: By collapsing individuals with ultra-rare predicted deleterious variants across multiple alleles, we enabled unbiased phenome-wide testing that revealed large effect sizes for multiple immune diagnoses.
Clinician-guided phenotyping in AoU and deep immunophenotyping in our referral cohort provided orthogonal validation.

The convergence of evidence across independent data sources demonstrates the power of rare variant collapsing approaches for diseases where individual variants are too rare for traditional association studies.
Future studies should explore whether similar patterns exist for diseases caused by other genetic mechanisms.
Our findings have immediate clinical implications.
Most importantly, our clinical biobank findings open a pathway to direct actionability through callback amendments to allow return-ofresults for confirmatory testing and improved treatment.
Such amendments have been successfully implemented across large biobanking consortia to return polygenic risk scores 37 and within the MGB Biobank for actionable genomic findings 38 .

text.text: Identification of potentially affected family members suggests that cascade testing could extend this impact.
Building on our findings, a return-of-results protocol for IEI is under evaluation at Mass General Brigham, to identify patients with as-yet undiagnosed and undertreated disease.

Outside of this immediate actionability, patients presenting with early-onset, multi-system, or treatment-refractory autoimmune and autoinflammatory disease should be considered for genetic testing, especially if they have features of Behcet's disease or unusual/atypical clinical presentations.
For patients with confirmed deleterious variants, proactive monitoring for disease development or progression is warranted.
This includes patients with hypomorphic missense variants, who are at high risk of clinically significant disease despite attenuated biomarker profiles.

text.text: The implications of these findings extend beyond HA20.

Recent work has identified monogenic disease in 1 to 3% of patients diagnosed with common inflammatory conditions like inflammatory bowel disease and multiple sclerosis, challenging the perception that monogenic conditions are ultra-rare and raising critical questions about prevalence and penetrance at a population level 1, 45 .

text.text: Our study addresses these questions directly, demonstrating higher than expected numbers and disease risk associations for most known haploinsufficiency IEI genes.

This gap between known and estimated disease prevalence may reflect ascertainment bias, poor access to genetic testing, or phenotypic heterogeneity: in HA20, patients may present with isolated autoimmune conditions rather than canonical HA20 phenotypes, leading to misclassification as a common polygenic disease.
Our findings suggest that rare IEI-HI variants may act as high-penetrance drivers or modify disease severity within ostensibly polygenic disease populations.
The heterogeneity and frequency of high-burden, multi-system immune disease in TNFAIP3 variant carriers suggests A20-related diseases may be particularly heterogeneous.
This may relate to A20's diverse regulatory functions, including ubiquitin-editing of the NF-κB, NLRP3, and type I interferon signaling pathways 44, [46] [47] [48] [49] .

text.text: Identifying the factors modulating expressivity and updating frameworks to account for phenotypic variability should be future priorities.
Our study has several limitations.
The referral HA20 cohort is subject to ascertainment bias and may not include individuals with incompletely penetrant variants or mild disease.
Conversely, EHR-based phenotyping used for population-wide analyses may be constrained by differences in site-specific data collection and coding practices 52 .

text.text: Moreover, AoU and UKBB exclusively include adult individuals, potentially limiting our ability to capture patients who may have developed early-onset severe disease.

Broad IEI-HI analyses relying on in silico predictors may imperfectly capture variant deleteriousness: >50% of HPPM variants were non-hypomorphic, and including benign or weakly hypomorphic variants could dilute observed associations.

Hence, it is possible that some excluded, functionally "normal" TNFAIP3 HPPM variants could have been deleterious, as seen for p.Gly583Glu.
Other variants could have been excluded based on computational prediction (e.g. c.2269C>A, p.Pro757Thr) or allele frequency (e.g. c.1033T>C, p.Tyr345His).

text.text: We mitigated these issues through stringent HPPM criteria, orthogonal phenotyping, domainspecific analyses, and concordant functional testing, but residual bias remains possible.
High throughput screens of TNFAIP3 function are needed to define the spectrum of A20 hypomorphism and variant pathogenicity at a population level.
We could not exclude deleterious variants in other immune genes in deleterious TNFAIP3 variant carriers or controls.
However, we confirmed the absence of co-occurring pLOF variants in other IEI-haploinsufficiency genes in both cohorts.
Other rare, incompletely penetrant variants, if present, would be expected to distribute comparably across groups.
Future work integrating functional validation, allele-specific expression studies, gene regulatory networks, and deep clinical phenotyping in large non-referral-based cohorts will be needed.

More broadly, existing analytical frameworks are optimized for extremes of allele frequency and risk effects: common, low-effect size variants for conventional GWAS/PheWAS and ultra-rare, extreme effect size variants for collapsing rare-variant analyses.
Moderately rare, moderately penetrant variants like c.1033T>C (p.Tyr345His) fall between these extremes, leading to inconclusive results when existing statistical frameworks are applied.

text.text: In summary, our findings integrate population genetics, functional validation, and clinical phenotyping to implicate TNFAIP3 hypomorphic variants as a substantially underrecognized driver of human disease, likely reflecting a broader pattern across haploinsufficiency immune diseases.

Expanded genetic testing, updated variant classification frameworks, and comprehensive clinical phenotyping may advance both the mechanistic understanding of monogenic diseases and the ability to diagnose affected individuals.

From a clinical standpoint, these approaches provide a concrete pathway to improved outcomes via return-of-results from existing biobanks, broad genetic testing, and pathway-directed therapies in tens of thousands of individuals with hypomorphic variants in TNFAIP3 and other immune signaling genes.
